title: Battle royale launch
like: a 100-player last-one-standing game on launch night
brief: On launch night millions of players queue for matches of 100. Each match streams positions many times a second, the lobby shows the live player count, and one patch notes page is opened by everyone. Connections must stay open, a match server dying must preserve acknowledged progress within the stated recovery point, and a few hot items, like the daily reward, are hit by everybody.

clarify.a: Within about 150 ms for players near the servers. Counting the trip across an ocean for everyone else, the target here is a 450 ms p99 (approx.).

clarify.q: If a match server dies, may the match be lost?
clarify.a: The match may be lost. At most the last 60 seconds of progress and rewards may need replay after a failure; earlier acknowledged progress must survive.

clarify.q: Can the lobby count be a little old?
clarify.a: Yes, a few seconds. It is the same number for everyone.

notes: A match has 100 players and sends about 10 position updates a second each (approx.).
Everyone opens the lobby count and the daily reward (approx.).
One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

numbers.label: Position updates per second at peak
Servers for the request and login calls
numbers.how: 15,000 × 0.35 other calls ÷ about 1,000 per server ≈ 5, plus room for the spike (approx.)

hints: Players stay connected for minutes. Which part holds a connection open, and which part answers the same question for everyone?
A socket gateway holds the connections and a pub/sub spreads positions inside a match. The lobby count and daily reward are one answer for everyone, so cache it.
Load balancer, socket gateway, pub/sub, servers, a cache for the hot items, a coordination service for who owns each match, and a wide-column store.

editorial.summary: Two kinds of traffic hide in one game: long-lived match connections that need a gateway and pub/sub, and a few hot read answers that one cache can absorb. Keeping them apart lets each be sized on its own.

designs.name: Socket gateway, pub/sub and a hot-item cache
designs.why: The gateway holds the connections and pub/sub fans positions out inside a match. The lobby count and daily reward come from a cache so the hot key never reaches the database, and a coordination service knows which server owns each match.

tradeoffs: Sending positions as small, frequent updates feels smooth but costs bandwidth; sending fewer, larger ones is cheaper and feels laggy.
A five second copy of the lobby count is invisible to players and removes almost all of that load.
Spreading a hot counter over several keys stops one partition from melting, at the price of adding them up when read.
Losing a match when its server dies is acceptable if progress and rewards are saved elsewhere.
editorial.realWorld: Launch nights for big online games reach millions of players at once; studios keep match state in memory and save only results to a database (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Battle royale launch: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
